newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Tensions high in polls crisis, Serbia awaits OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Tensions high in polls crisis, Serbia awaits OSCE.

text.p: Embattled Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and defiant opposition protesters refused to back down on Thursday as both sides awaited an international delegation due to discuss disputed local election results.

The Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition vowed to continue their daily mass rallies across Serbia until their victories in November local elections were recognised. Milosevic has refused to reinstate the annulled poll triumphs.

Felipe Gonzalez, a former Spanish premier, will head a team from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe invited in by Milosevic to try and resolve a crisis which is shaking his grip on power. It is expected to arrive on Friday.

"The OSCE mission is expected to contribute to the settlement of the doubts that have arisen over a small number of mandates which are disputed in the local elections," Serbian Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic told reporters.
"Whatever it decides will be run through our institutions," said Milutinovic, without elaborating.

In his first comment on the 32 straight days of mass demonstrations which have revived memories of the 1989 revolutions which rocked Eastern Europe, Milutinovic said the local election results had been blown up out of all proportion.
"The reaction is totally out of proportion to the issue," he said, adding the issue could be solved by negotiations.
"The opposition has made a point by street demonstrations but it is time to get on with more important matters, like re-building the economy," he said.
Milutinovic's public acknowledgement of the dispute comes after Milosevic, who initially remained aloof, said on Tuesday he would investigate the accusations of vote rigging.

Political sources believe that Milosevic has now abandoned his sit-it-out tactics and, due to Washington-led international criticism and the sheer size of the rallies, is preparing to distance himself from any electoral irregularities.
Under tough Western scrutiny Milosevic has kept his security forces away from the protests. In 1991 he sent tanks to crush big demonstrations.
Zajedno is adamant it will keep up daily rallies until victories it claims in 15 of Serbia's biggest towns and cities including Belgrade are recognised.
The scale of its support has stoked its determination.
"You can see that the regime is starting to give way, the cracks are much bigger than we expected," opposition leader Zoran Djindjic told a Belgrade rally on Wednesday.
"We do not now want to slip through those cracks, we want to topple the entire wall," he said to cheers.

The spirit of protest is being fuelled by inventive themes and on Thursday Zajedno was laying on a feast with fried fish, cakes and wine for its supporters to celebrate St Nikolas's day in central Belgrade.
Another student protest march arrived in the capital on Thursday after walking in from the southern industrial town of Kragujevac and were greeted with cheers and firecrackers.
They joined a daily student march of about 30,000 people walking around Belgrade carrying banners saying "Better Dead than Red", "We Still Exist When You Can't See Us" and "This is Local Freedom".
